text: Most men and most women, including the ones who call themselves feminists, do not understand what feminism is, where it comes from, and how did it change along the way. We have a lot of myths and legends around it. This is why I continue with my series Mansplaining Feminism. And before we even start with the first wave of feminism, we need to understand the world feminism came from. For most of history, life wasn't easy for anyone. The vast majority of people were poor, powerless, and had very limited access to education or political influence. Most men were not living some comfortable, privileged life. They were working, fighting, surviving, and dealing with strict class systems themselves. But women had an additional layer of limitation. For men, many barriers were based on class and status. For women, there was another barrier on top of that – gender itself. Even a woman with status could still be excluded from education, politics, professions, or basic legal independence. And this is where the story becomes interesting. Because as society slowly began questioning power, authority, class, religion, rights, and freedom, some voices also started asking, what about women? If we are talking about reason, education, dignity, and human worth, do women count too? And that question didn't appear out of nowhere. Already in 1405, Christine de Pizan writes the Book of the City of Ladies, where she pushes back against the idea that women are naturally inferior. She argues that maybe the problem is not women, but the way they've been described for centuries. And that was a serious argument for that time. Then, over the next centuries, Europe has what is called the Curelle de Femme, the woman question. This was a long debate about women's intelligence, morality, education, and role in society. In other words, people were already arguing about whether women were naturally inferior, or whether society simply treated them that way. Then, in the late 18th century, everything accelerates. You have the American Revolution and the French Revolution. And for the first time, ideas like liberty, equality, rights, and citizenship are not just philosophical. They become political. They become the foundation of entire societies. And once you start saying things like, all men are equal, and people have natural rights, one question becomes impossible to ignore. Does that include women? And now the argument becomes much more direct. In 1791, Olav de Gouge takes the famous Declaration of the Rights of Men and rewrites it as the Declaration of the Rights of Woman, basically saying, if you believe in rights, apply them consistently. And just a year later, in 1792, Mary Wollstonecraft publishes A Vindication of the Rights of Woman. And her argument is very clear. Women are not inferior by nature. They appear inferior because they are denied education and opportunity, which is a very direct challenge to how society was structured. And this is the key point. Before feminism became a movement, it was already a question. A question that kept coming back for centuries. If women are rational human beings, if they can think, learn, contribute, and take responsibility, then why are they being excluded from education, rights, and public life? And once that question enters the conversation, it does not just disappear. It grows. It moves from books, debates, and philosophical arguments into petitions, campaigns, organizations, and political pressure. And that is where we finally arrive at what we now call the first wave of feminism. This is when the conversation stops being only about defending women in theory and starts becoming about changing laws in practice. Voting rights, property rights, education, legal recognition. And that is what we're going to talk about in the next part.
